title: Chaos Engineering
description: Learn steady-state hypothesis, Chaos Monkey, Litmus, fault injection techniques, GameDay exercises, and Netflix's chaos engineering culture.

segments.text: Your system passes all tests, monitoring is green, and you're confident it handles failures. Then AWS us-east-1 has a partial outage and your service crashes. Chaos engineering proactively injects failures in production to discover weaknesses before they cause real outages. Netflix's philosophy: if something is going to break, break it on your terms, during business hours, with your team watching.

Every chaos experiment starts with a steady-state hypothesis. Define what normal looks like: p99 latency under two hundred milliseconds, error rate below zero point one percent, orders processed per minute above one thousand. Then inject a failure and verify the steady state holds. If it doesn't, you've found a resilience gap to fix.

Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production instances. Netflix runs it during business hours — if a single instance death breaks your service, your architecture is wrong. It forces teams to build for redundancy: every service must handle instance failures gracefully. After years of Chaos Monkey, Netflix services survive individual instance failures without any user impact.

Fault injection categories: infrastructure — kill pods, terminate nodes, fill disks. Network — add latency, drop packets, partition networks. Application — inject exceptions, corrupt responses, slow database queries. State — delete cache entries, corrupt queue messages. Each category tests different resilience mechanisms. Start with infrastructure faults — they're safest and most impactful.

Your team wants to inject a two-hundred-millisecond network delay between your payment service and the database in production. The VP is nervous about impacting real customers. How do you make a case for this experiment and minimize blast radius?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you convince leadership to allow chaos experiments in production? What safety guardrails?

segments.text: LitmusChaos is an open-source chaos engineering platform for Kubernetes. It provides pre-built experiments: pod delete, container kill, node drain, network loss, disk fill. Experiments are defined as CRDs — Custom Resource Definitions — making them version-controlled and repeatable. Probes verify the steady-state hypothesis automatically during the experiment.

GameDay exercises are scheduled chaos engineering events. The team picks a failure scenario, defines the hypothesis, runs the experiment, and documents findings — all in a few hours. Google runs regular DiRT — Disaster Recovery Testing — exercises that simulate regional outages. The learning from one GameDay often prevents multiple future outages.

Blast radius control is essential. Start small: one pod, one user, one region. Use feature flags to limit the experiment scope. Have a kill switch that immediately stops the experiment. Monitor user-facing metrics in real-time. Netflix's Chaos Automation Platform automatically aborts experiments when error rates exceed predefined thresholds.

Chaos engineering is a culture, not a tool. Netflix's Simian Army includes Chaos Monkey, Latency Monkey, Conformity Monkey, and Chaos Kong — which simulates entire region failures. The culture shift: failure is expected, not exceptional. Teams that embrace chaos engineering have fifty percent fewer production incidents because they've already found and fixed the weak points.
Design a chaos engineering program for a company with two hundred microservices that has never done chaos engineering before. What's your six-month roadmap from zero to production chaos experiments?
segments.thought_prompt: Design a 6-month chaos engineering roadmap for a company starting from zero.

segments.text: Chaos engineering proactively discovers resilience gaps by injecting controlled failures. Start with a steady-state hypothesis, use tools like Chaos Monkey and Litmus for execution, control blast radius with automated abort, and build the culture through regular GameDay exercises. The Staff-level principle: a system that hasn't been tested for failure hasn't been tested at all.
